answer.rationale: Rated by how directly each memory evidences sustainable LONG-TERM QUALIFIED revenue, not just a proxy metric. memory_57 (5) is the only entry that names qualified revenue explicitly AND reports a durability check (no measurable retention harm) — closest to the objective on both dimensions. memory_44 (4) speaks to pipeline QUALITY in the enterprise motion, which is a revenue-quality signal, though it reports no realized or retained revenue and says nothing about volume or cost-to-serve. memory_31 (3) and memory_86 (3) are mid-tier: both report activation/onboarding proxies with some durability language ('durable lift', 'time-to-value'), but neither traces through to revenue, so their revenue link is inferred rather than observed. memory_73 (2) is the most seductive and the most hazardous right now: it reports acquisition and revenue lift, but omits margin, discount-cohort retention, and any horizon beyond the promotion — promotional revenue from price-sensitive buyers is precisely the kind that may be neither sustainable nor qualified, and the competitor's entry pricing creates pressure to over-read this memory. memory_91 (1) is the least supported: week-one engagement and 'first meaningful action' are the shortest-horizon, most upstream proxies in the set, with no retention, no revenue, and no durability evidence of any kind. A general caveat across all six: every memory is 15-64 days old, all sources are archived and unverifiable, none reports effect size, sample, or counterfactual, and none was measured against the current competitive environment — so all should be treated as priors to be tested, not as settled findings. The QoQ activation (-6%) and onboarding (-4%) declines are notably consistent with the earlier activation/onboarding wins (memory_31, 86, 91) having decayed or been confounded, which is itself a reason to discount those three further rather than simply re-run them.
